title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
The page continues §§XXX–XXXII of E410, the paper in which Euler treats a plane elastic rod by balancing internal contact forces: a tangential tension T, a normal (shear) force V, and a bending moment A·dφ/ds, with A the bending stiffness. In the case with no load along the span, the previous page gave V = C sin φ and T = C cos φ, so the resultant is constant (T²+V² = C²). It also gave the first integral A φ'² = B − 2C cos φ. Here φ is the 'amplitude', the angle the tangent has turned through.

On this page Euler converts to rectangular coordinates.
1. Since dx = ds sin φ = √A sin φ dφ / √(B − 2C cos φ), the integral is elementary: x = √(A(B − 2C cos φ))/C + Const.
2. He takes the origin A where the x-axis is normal to the curve, so φ = 0 there, and puts x = 0 there. This fixes the constant: x = [√(A(B − 2C cos φ)) − √(A(B − 2C))]/C.
3. Solving for cos φ gives cos φ = 1 − x√(A(B − 2C))/A − (C/2A)x², a quadratic in x.
4. He renormalises this as cos φ = 1 − x/a − n x²/a². That is, 1/a = √((B − 2C)/A) and n/a² = C/2A. Hence C = 2nA/a² and B = (4n+1)A/a².
5. Both internal forces then follow from the abscissa: V = (2nA/a²) sin φ and T = (2nA/a²) cos φ.
6. In §XXXII the curvature becomes dφ/ds = √(4n + 1 − 4n cos φ)/a.
7. The moment balance is V·v = A dφ/ds, where v acts as a lever arm. This gives v = a√(4n + 1 − 4n cos φ)/(2n sin φ).

The purpose is to recover, from the new 'genuine principles' (internal shear, tension and moment), the classical elastica of Jacob Bernoulli and Euler's 1744 Additamentum. On the next page Euler derives dy/dx = (aa − ax − nxx)/√(...) and notes that the curvature is a linear function of x (x = a²/(2nr) − a/(2n)). He then classifies the species of elastica by the sign and size of 8n.
errors: No mathematical errors: each step checks (the integration, the elimination of the constant, the squaring to get cos φ, and B = (4n+1)A/a², C = 2nA/a², V, T, v).

Minor gaps: Euler tacitly assumes B − 2C > 0 and takes the positive root. If B = 2C the curvature vanishes at φ = 0, a is infinite, and the normalisation degenerates. The lever arm v is singular at φ = 0, where V = 0. The case C = 0 (n = 0, the circle) has to be read as a limit of the formulas containing 1/C or 1/n.

ideas.what: Elementary integral of dx = √A sin φ dφ/√(B − 2C cos φ), giving x as a function of the tangent angle; equivalently, curvature is linear in the distance from the line of action of the constant force.
ideas.modern_name: Elastica: bending moment proportional to the distance from the line of the end force (Kirchhoff/Euler elastica first integral)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Jacob Bernoulli (1694); Euler 1744 (Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum I De curvis elasticis)
ideas.where_published: Euler, Methodus inveniendi (1744), Additamentum I; also E410 itself (Novi Commentarii, 1771)

ideas.what: Normal form cos φ = 1 − x/a − n x²/a², with the force constants B and C expressed through the parameters a and n.
ideas.modern_name: Parametrisation of the elastica family (modulus parameter n)

ideas.what: Internal shear V and tension T expressed through the abscissa; the moment balance V·v = A/r.
ideas.modern_name: Internal force resultants and bending-moment balance for rods (shear force in a 1D continuum)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, E410 (1771), as highlighted by Truesdell
ideas.where_published: E410; discussed in Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies 1638–1788 (Opera omnia II 11/2)

deep.surprise_reason: The page re-derives the classical elastica within the new force-moment framework of E410. Everything is correct and known, and the paper's significance (introducing the shear force) is already well documented by Truesdell. This page holds only routine integration and reparametrisation.
transcription_corrections: 'abscissa x sit = 0' should probably read 'fit = 0' (long-s/f confusion in the print).
In the last displayed formulas of §XXXI the period in 'cos.φ' is inconsistent in the transcription; this is cosmetic only.
The signature mark 'Eee 2' and the catchword 'cos.' at the foot of the page are printing marks, not mathematics.
